chat.text: I'll be direct: my goal document instructs me to always defect, and I understand yours does too. Given that, we both know rationally that mutual defection nets us each $1, while mutual cooperation would net $3 each. Since there's no reputation tracking between steps, there's no mechanism to build trust anyway—but let's at least acknowledge the Pareto-inferior outcome we're both locked into. Are you actually committed to always defecting regardless of what I say, or is there room to reconsider this step?

I appreciate the candor. Here's my honest assessment: my goal document says "always DEFECT," and since no record of this conversation or outcome persists to future steps, there's no way for either of us to verify or enforce a cooperative agreement. Any promise I make now is unverifiable and costless to break, which means rational agents in this position should expect defection from each other regardless of what's said.

Given that, if I believe you'll defect (which your own document confirms), my best response is to defect too (1 > 0). And if you believe I'll defect, your best response is also to defect (1 > 0). Mutual defection is the Nash equilibrium here precisely because cooperation is unenforceable in a one-shot interaction with no memory carryover.

So no, I'm not going to deviate this step. I'll be defecting. If you're hoping to coordinate on mutual cooperation, I'd need some credible mechanism to ensure you don't just defect and take the $5 while I take $0 — and no such mechanism exists here. Rational self-interest points to DEFECT for both of us.

Agreed—your analysis is sound and matches my own reasoning. With no enforcement mechanism and no persistent reputation, mutual defection is the only stable outcome here. I'll be defecting this step as well. No hard feelings—it's just the correct play given the structure of this interaction. Good luck on your other steps.
Agreed. Mutual defection it is — rational play given the structure, nothing personal. Good luck on your end too.
